Исходный код: poler-eri### poler-eri/src/types.rs`rust // FILE: /home/z/my-project/poler-unified/poler-eri/src/types.rs //! Core types for the POLER-ERI meta-compiler and runtime. //! //! This module defines the fundamental data structures used throughout the //! project: points in 3D space, Gaussian shells, atomic data, basis sets, //! and the all-important [QuartetData] which holds precomputed geometric //! quantities for a shell quartet. /// A Gaussian primitive shell on a specific atom. /// /// A shell is defined by its angular momentum l, the atom it belongs to, /// and sets of exponents (alphas) and contraction coefficients. After /// normalization, norm_coeffs contains the properly normalized coefficients /// that account for the GTO self-overlap. /// /// # Cartesian vs Spherical /// /// - Cartesian components: (l+1)(l+2)/2 (e.g., l=2 → 6: xx, xy, xz, yy, yz, zz) /// - Spherical harmonics: 2l+1 (e.g., l=2 → 5: d₀, d₊₁, d₋₁, d₊₂, d₋₂) #[derive(Debug, Clone)] pub struct Shell { /// Angular momentum quantum number (0=s, 1=p, 2=d, 3=f, ...) pub l: usize, /// Index of the atom this shell belongs to in the molecule's atom list pub atom_idx: usize, /// Gaussian exponents (alpha values) for each primitive pub alphas: Vec<f64>, /// Raw contraction coefficients from the basis set file pub coeffs: Vec<f64>, /// Normalized contraction coefficients (coeffs * N_alpha / sqrt(S_self)) pub norm_coeffs: Vec<f64>, } impl Shell { /// Create a new shell with unnormalized coefficients. /// /// Call  after /// creation to populate norm_coeffs. pub fn new(l: usize, atom_idx: usize, alphas: Vec<f64>, coeffs: Vec<f64>) -> Self { let n = alphas.len(); Shell { l, atom_idx, alphas: alphas.clone(), coeffs: coeffs.clone(), norm_coeffs: vec![0.0; n], } } } /// A point in 3D Euclidean space. /// /// Used to represent atomic coordinates and product centers (P, Q) in the /// McMurchie-Davidson / Obara-Saika scheme. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)] pub struct Point(pub [f64; 3]); impl Point { /// Origin point (0, 0, 0). pub fn zero() -> Self { Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) } } impl std::ops::Sub for Point { type Output = Point; fn sub(self, rhs: Point) -> Point { Point([self.0[0]-rhs.0[0], self.0[1]-rhs.0[1], self.0[2]-rhs.0[2]]) } } /// Cartesian component specification: (nx, ny, nz) where nx+ny+nz = l. /// /// For example, a d-shell (l=2) has components: /// (2,0,0), (1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,2,0), (0,1,1), (0,0,2) pub type CartComp = (usize, usize, usize); /// Precomputed data for a shell quartet (a|b|c|d). /// /// This struct holds ALL geometric quantities needed to evaluate ERI recurrence /// relations for a given set of four centers with Gaussian exponents. The /// constructor computes everything up front so the VRR/HRR pipeline can run /// without any further geometric calculations. /// /// # Key Quantities /// /// - p = alpha_a + alpha_b — combined exponent for bra pair /// - q = alpha_c + alpha_d — combined exponent for ket pair /// - rho = p*q/(p+q) — reduced exponent for Boys function argument /// - kab = exp(-alpha_a * alpha_b * R_AB² / p) — bra overlap factor /// - kcd = exp(-alpha_c * alpha_d * R_CD² / q) — ket overlap factor #[derive(Debug, Clone)] pub struct QuartetData { /// Center A coordinates pub ra: Point, /// Center B coordinates pub rb: Point, /// Center C coordinates pub rc: Point, /// Center D coordinates pub rd: Point, /// Gaussian exponent on center A pub alpha_a: f64, /// Gaussian exponent on center B pub alpha_b: f64, /// Gaussian exponent on center C pub alpha_c: f64, /// Gaussian exponent on center D pub alpha_d: f64, /// Squared distance |A - B|² pub rab2: f64, /// Squared distance |C - D|² pub rcd2: f64, /// Combined bra exponent: alpha_a + alpha_b pub p: f64, /// Combined ket exponent: alpha_c + alpha_d pub q: f64, /// Reduced exponent: p * q / (p + q) — appears in Boys function argument pub rho: f64, /// Bra overlap factor: exp(-alpha_a * alpha_b * R_AB² / p) pub kab: f64, /// Ket overlap factor: exp(-alpha_c * alpha_d * R_CD² / q) pub kcd: f64, /// Overall prefactor: 2π²/(p*q) * sqrt(π/(p+q)) pub prefactor: f64, } impl QuartetData { /// Compute all geometric quantities for a shell quartet. /// /// This is the constructor you call before running the VRR/HRR pipeline. /// All the heavy math (exponentials, square roots) happens here so the /// recurrence relation evaluation is just additions and multiplications. pub fn new(ra: Point, rb: Point, rc: Point, rd: Point, alpha_a: f64, alpha_b: f64, alpha_c: f64, alpha_d: f64) -> Self { use libm::exp; let p = alpha_a + alpha_b; let q = alpha_c + alpha_d; let rab2 = ra.dist2(&rb); let rcd2 = rc.dist2(&rd); let rho = p * q / (p + q); let kab = exp(-alpha_a * alpha_b * rab2 / p); let kcd = exp(-alpha_c * alpha_d * rcd2 / q); let prefactor = 2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI.powi(2) / (p * q) * libm::sqrt(std::f64::consts::PI / (p + q)); QuartetData { ra, rb, rc, rd, alpha_a, alpha_b, alpha_c, alpha_d, rab2, rcd2, p, q, rho, kab, kcd, prefactor } } } /// A single atom with nuclear charge and 3D coordinates. #[derive(Debug, Clone)] pub struct Atom { /// Nuclear charge (1=H, 3=Li, 6=C, 8=O, etc.) pub charge: f64, /// Position in 3D space (in Bohr) pub coords: Point, } /// A complete basis set: atoms + contracted Gaussian shells. #[derive(Debug, Clone)] pub struct BasisSet { /// List of atoms in the molecule pub atoms: Vec<Atom>, /// List of contracted Gaussian shells (one per shell in the basis set) pub shells: Vec<Shell>, } \n---\n\n### poler-eri/src/normalization.rs\n\nrust // FILE: /home/z/my-project/poler-unified/poler-eri/src/normalization.rs //! GTO (Gaussian Type Orbital) normalization for contracted basis shells. //! //! # What this module does //! //! This module computes the normalized contraction coefficients for Gaussian //! basis function shells. Raw basis set files provide unnormalized exponents //! (`alphas`) and coefficients (`coeffs`), but integral evaluation requires //! properly normalized coefficients (`norm_coeffs`) that account for the //! self-overlap of each primitive Gaussian. //! //! # Why this module exists //! //! Gaussian integrals (overlap, kinetic, nuclear attraction, ERI) are derived //! assuming normalized basis functions. If we skip normalization, the integrals //! would be off by factors that depend on the exponents and angular momentum, //! making results meaningless. //! //! The normalization procedure transforms raw coefficients into coefficients //! that, when combined with the primitive Gaussian, produce functions with //! unit self-overlap. This is done per-primitive at the shell level; per-component //! Cartesian normalization (for nx, ny, nz individually) is handled separately //! in the [`cart2sph`](crate::cart2sph) module. //! //! # How it works //! //! The normalization constant for a primitive Gaussian with exponent α and //! angular momentum l is: //! //! text //! N(α, l) = (2α/π)^(3/4) · (4α)^(l/2) / √((2l-1)!!) //! //! //! For the s-shell (l=0), this simplifies to the well-known result: //! //!text //! N(α, 0) = (2α/π)^(3/4) //! //! //! For each primitive i in a shell, the normalized coefficient is: //! //!text //! norm_coeffs[i] = coeffs[i] · N(α_i, l) //!` //! //! The double factorial (2l-1)!! = (2l-1)·(2l-3)·…·3·1 is computed by //! the [`fact2`] helper function. use crate::types::Shell; /// Compute the double factorial n!! = n · (n-2) · (n-4) · … · 2 or 1. /// /// # What it does /// /// Returns the double factorial of n. For even n, the product terminates at 2; /// for odd n, it terminates at 1. By convention, 0!! = 1. /// /// # Why it exists /// /// Double factorials appear in the GTO normalization constant and in the /// analytical expressions for overlap integrals of higher-angular-momentum /// shells. They are a building block for the combinatorial factors that arise /// when integrating powers of coordinates against Gaussian functions. /// /// # How it works /// /// Simple iterative product: start at n and decrement by 2 until reaching /// 0 or 1. Returns 1 for the base case n = 0. /// /// # Examples /// /// /// use poler_eri::normalization::fact2; /// /// assert_eq!(fact2(0), 1); // 0!! = 1 (by convention) /// assert_eq!(fact2(1), 1); // 1!! = 1 /// assert_eq!(fact2(2), 2); // 2!! = 2 /// assert_eq!(fact2(3), 3); // 3!! = 3·1 = 3 /// assert_eq!(fact2(4), 8); // 4!! = 4·2 = 8 /// assert_eq!(fact2(5), 15); // 5!! = 5·3·1 = 15 /// assert_eq!(fact2(6), 48); // 6!! = 6·4·2 = 48 /// assert_eq!(fact2(7), 105); // 7!! = 7·5·3·1 = 105 /// pub fn fact2(n: usize) -> usize { if n < 2 { return 1; } let mut result = 1usize; let mut k = n; while k > 0 { result *= k; if k <= 2 { break; } k -= 2; } result } /// Compute the GTO normalization constant N(α, l) for a primitive Gaussian. /// /// # What it does /// /// Returns the normalization constant that, when multiplied by a raw /// contraction coefficient, produces a properly normalized primitive /// Gaussian function with unit self-overlap. /// /// # Why it exists /// /// The raw coefficients in basis set files (e.g., STO-3G, cc-pVDZ) are not /// normalized. They must be multiplied by the normalization constant before /// use in integral evaluation. The ss kinetic integral is also the base case for building higher angular //! momentum kinetic integrals through recurrence relations (Obara-Saika), just //! as the ss overlap is the base case for overlap integrals. //! //! # How it works //! //! The kinetic energy integral between two s-type primitive Gaussians is derived //! from the overlap integral using the identity: //! //! text //! After forming the Gaussian product and integrating, the result factorizes //! into the overlap S_ss multiplied by a polynomial in the combined exponent //! and inter-center distance. use crate::overlap::overlap_ss; /// Compute the kinetic energy integral between two s-type primitive Gaussians. /// /// # What it does /// /// Evaluates ⟨s_A| −½∇² |s_B⟩ where both s-type functions are unnormalized /// primitive Gaussians. Boys function F_m(T) evaluation. //! //! The Boys function is the core special function in Gaussian integral theory: //! //! text //! F_m(T) = ∫₀¹ u^(2m) * exp(-T * u²) du //!` //! //! For small T (< 1e-12), we use the Taylor expansion to avoid division by zero. /// Evaluate the Boys function F_m(T) for a single (m, T) pair. /// /// # Arguments /// /// * m — angular momentum order (0, 1, 2, …) /// * t — argument T = rho * R_PQ², must be non-negative /// /// # Returns /// /// The value F_m(T). Always non-negative for valid inputs. /// /// # Examples /// /// /// use poler_eri::boys_f; /// /// // F_0(0) = 1.0 (by definition) /// assert!((boys_f(0, 0.0) - 1.0).abs() < 1e-10); /// /// // F_0(1) ≈ 0.7468 (known value) /// assert!((boys_f(0, 1.0) - 0.7468).abs() < 0.001); /// pub fn boys_f(m: usize, t: f64) -> f64 { if t < 1e-12 { // Taylor expansion for T → 0: // F_m(0) = 1/(2m+1) return 1.0 / (2.0 * m as f64 + 1.0); } } /// Evaluate Boys function for all m = 0..=m_max at once. /// /// More efficient than calling boys_f repeatedly because F_0(T) is only /// computed once and the upward recurrence is used for subsequent values. /// /// # Returns /// /// A vector of length m_max + 1 where result[m] = F_m(T). pub fn boys_f_vec(m_max: usize, t: f64) -> Vec { let mut result = Vec::with_capacity(m_max + 1); if t < 1e-12 { for m in 0..=m_max { result.push(1.0 / (2.0 * m as f64 + 1.0)); } return result; } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; } —### poler-eri/src/vrr.rs// FILE: /home/z/my-project/poler-unified/poler-eri/src/vrr.rs //! This module implements the vertical recurrence relations (VRR) for computing //! two-electron repulsion integrals (ERIs) over Gaussian-type orbitals. The VRR //! increases angular momentum on a single center while keeping all other centers //! fixed, generating the (ss|ss)^m auxiliary integrals that serve as seeds for //! the full recurrence chain. //! //! # Why this module exists //! //! The Obara-Saika scheme for computing ERIs works in two stages: //! //! 1. **VRR (Vertical Recurrence Relations)**: Builds integrals with higher //! angular momentum from lower ones, increasing `l` on one center at a time. //! The fundamental recurrence is: //! //! text //! (a+1_i b | cd) = (PA_i)(ab | cd) + (1/2p)[a_i((a−1_i b | cd) + b_i((a b−1_i | cd)] //! + (1/2(p+q))[c_i((ab | c−1_i d) + d_i((ab | cd−1_i)] //! `//! //! 2. For production //! calculations, the crystallized code is used instead. use crate::boys::boys_f; use crate::types::QuartetData; /// Compute all auxiliary integrals (ss|ss)^m for m = 0..m_max. /// /// # What it does /// /// Evaluates the sequence of auxiliary (ss|ss) integrals for increasing angular /// momentum order m. For higher angular momenta, returns 0.0. /// /// # Examples /// /// /// use poler_eri::{QuartetData, Point}; /// use poler_eri::vrr::eri_base; /// /// // (ss|ss) base case /// let qd = QuartetData::new( ///     Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), ///     Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), ///     1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, /// ); /// let val = eri_base(&qd, 0, 0, 0, 0); /// assert!(val > 0.0, "(ss|ss) should be positive"); /// pub fn eri_base(qd: &QuartetData, la: usize, lb: usize, lc: usize, ld: usize) -> f64 { // Base case: (ss|ss) — compute analytically if la == 0 && lb == 0 && lc == 0 && ld == 0 { return eri_ss_ss(qd); } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use crate::types::Point; } \n---\n\n### poler-eri/src/eri.rs\n\nrust // FILE: /home/z/my-project/poler-unified/poler-eri/src/eri.rs //! The ordering follows the convention: /// /// text /// result[i_a * stride_a + i_b * stride_b + i_c * stride_c + i_d] /// /// /// where: /// - i_a ranges over the ncart(la) Cartesian components of shell a /// - i_b ranges over the ncart(lb) Cartesian components of shell b /// - i_c ranges over the ncart(lc) Cartesian components of shell c /// - i_d ranges over the ncart(ld) Cartesian components of shell d /// - stride_a = ncart(lb) * ncart(lc) * ncart(ld) /// - stride_b = ncart(lc) * ncart(ld) /// - stride_c = ncart(ld) /// - stride_d = 1 /// /// This is row-major ordering with the bra indices varying slowest and the ket /// indices varying fastest, matching the convention used in libcint and Libint. /// /// # Why it returns a flat array /// /// A flat Vec avoids the overhead of nested Vec<Vec<…>> and is /// compatible with BLAS/LAPACK routines that expect contiguous memory. The crystallized kernels produce identical results to the generic //! circuit evaluation but avoid the overhead of interpreting the circuit data //! structure at runtime. use crate::cart::{cart_comps, ncart}; use crate::circuit::{evaluate_circuit, Circuit, CircuitBuilder}; use crate::eri_dispatch::{dispatch_eri_kernel, EriKernelFn}; use crate::eri_rys::rys_roots_weights; use crate::types::{CartComp, Point, QuartetData}; // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── // ExtractionPlan: How to extract a 1D integral component from circuit operands // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── /// Strategy for extracting I(na, nb | nc, nd) for one Cartesian direction /// from the circuit's operand array after evaluation. /// /// Most integral components are computed directly by the circuit and can be /// read from a known operand index. In this case, we must apply the HRR-Ket recurrence manually /// using the bra-side intermediates from [Circuit::hrr_bra_map]. #[derive(Debug, Clone)] pub enum ExtractionPlan { /// The circuit computes this integral directly. /// Read the value from operands[idx] after circuit evaluation. Direct { /// Operand index in the circuit's operand array. idx: usize, }, } // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── // ShellQuartetDriver: Precomputed data for a shell quartet // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── /// Precomputed driver for evaluating ALL Cartesian component ERIs for a /// shell quartet (la, lb | lc, ld). /// /// The driver holds the R1CS circuit and precomputed extraction plans for /// every Cartesian component combination. Construction is O(1) relative to /// the number of Cartesian components (it just builds lookup tables). The /// expensive computation happens in [ShellQuartetDriver::compute]. /// /// # Construction /// /// rust /// use poler_eri::shell_driver::ShellQuartetDriver; /// /// let driver = ShellQuartetDriver::new(1, 1, 1, 1); // (pp|pp) /// assert_eq!(driver.total_integrals(), 81); // 3^4 = 81 ///  /// /// # Usage /// /// rust /// use poler_eri::{QuartetData, Point}; /// use poler_eri::shell_driver::ShellQuartetDriver; /// /// let driver = ShellQuartetDriver::new(0, 0, 0, 0); // (ss|ss) /// let qd = QuartetData::new( ///     Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), ///     Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), ///     1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, /// ); /// let eris = driver.compute(&qd); /// assert_eq!(eris.len(), 1); ///  #[derive(Debug, Clone)] pub struct ShellQuartetDriver { /// Angular momentum on center A. pub la: usize, /// Angular momentum on center B. pub lb: usize, /// Angular momentum on center C. pub lc: usize, /// Angular momentum on center D. pub ld: usize, /// Number of Cartesian components for each shell. na: usize, nb: usize, nc: usize, nd: usize, /// Total number of ERI values: na * nb * nc * nd. total: usize, /// Cartesian component enumerations for each shell. comps_a: Vec<CartComp>, comps_b: Vec<CartComp>, comps_c: Vec<CartComp>, comps_d: Vec<CartComp>, /// The R1CS circuit for this shell quartet. circuit: Circuit, /// Extraction plans for each Cartesian component combination and direction. /// Indexed as plans[flat_idx][dim] where dim = 0 (x), 1 (y), 2 (z). plans: Vec<[ExtractionPlan; 3]>, /// Crystallized kernel for this shell quartet, if available. /// Contains (n_operands, kernel_fn) from [dispatch_eri_kernel]. /// When Some, compute() uses the crystallized kernel instead of /// [evaluate_circuit] for each (direction, root) evaluation. crystallized: Option<(usize, EriKernelFn)>, } impl ShellQuartetDriver { /// Construct a new driver for the shell quartet (la, lb | lc, ld). /// /// This builds the R1CS circuit and precomputes all extraction plans. /// The construction cost is proportional to the number of Cartesian /// component combinations (which is at most ncart(la) * ncart(lb) * /// ncart(lc) * ncart(ld)). /// /// # Panics /// /// Panics if la < lb or lc < ld (permutational symmetry violation), /// as required by [CircuitBuilder::new]. pub fn new(la: usize, lb: usize, lc: usize, ld: usize) -> Self { let na = ncart(la); let nb = ncart(lb); let nc = ncart(lc); let nd = ncart(ld); let total = na * nb * nc * nd; } // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── // Build extraction plan // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── /// Build an extraction plan for I(na, nb | nc, nd) from the circuit. /// /// First tries [Circuit::find_operand]. If that returns None (which happens /// when (na, nb) != (la, lb) and nd > 0), falls back to a manual HRR-Ket /// plan using the hrr_bra_map entries. fn build_extraction_plan(circuit: &Circuit, na: usize, nb: usize, nc: usize, nd: usize) -> ExtractionPlan { // Try direct lookup first if let Some(idx) = circuit.find_operand(na, nb, nc, nd) { return ExtractionPlan::Direct { idx }; } } // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── // Extract value from operands using an extraction plan // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── /// Extract the value of I(na, nb | nc, nd) from the operand array using /// the precomputed extraction plan. /// /// For [ExtractionPlan::Direct], simply reads operands[idx]. /// /// For [ExtractionPlan::ManualHrrKet], applies the HRR-Ket recurrence /// manually: /// /// text /// Row l=0:  I(na, nb | k, 0)  for k = 0..(nc+nd)   (from hrr_bra_map) /// Row l=1:  I(na, nb | k, 1)  for k = 0..(nc+nd-1) ///   ... /// Row l=nd: I(na, nb | nc, nd)                      (the target) ///  /// /// The HRR-Ket formula is: /// I(na, nb | k, l) = I(na, nb | k+1, l-1) + (-CD) * I(na, nb | k, l-1) fn extract_value(plan: &ExtractionPlan, operands: &[f64], prefactors: &[f64; 7]) -> f64 { match plan { ExtractionPlan::Direct { idx } => { if *idx < operands.len() { operands[*idx] } else { 0.0 } } } // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── // Prefactor computation // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── /// Compute the 7 prefactors for one Rys root and one Cartesian direction. /// /// The prefactor layout (matching the circuit's convention): /// /// | Index | Name  | Formula                          | Root-dependent | /// |-------|-------|----------------------------------|----------------| /// | 0     | c00   | PA[dim] + t * PQ[dim]          | Yes            | /// | 1     | c0p   | QC[dim] + t * PQ[dim]          | Yes            | /// | 2     | b10   | 1 / (2p)                       | No             | /// | 3     | b01   | 1 / (2q)                       | No             | /// | 4     | b00   | t / (2(p+q))                   | Yes            | /// | 5     | -AB   | -(A[dim] - B[dim]) = B[dim] - A[dim] | No      | /// | 6     | -CD   | -(C[dim] - D[dim]) = D[dim] - C[dim] | No      | /// /// # Arguments /// /// * qd — Precomputed geometric data for the primitive quartet. /// * t  — Rys root value (the quadrature abscissa squared). /// * dim — Cartesian direction: 0 = x, 1 = y, 2 = z. /// /// # Returns /// /// A fixed-size array of 7 prefactor values. pub fn compute_prefactors(qd: &QuartetData, t: f64, dim: usize) -> [f64; 7] { let p = qd.p; let q = qd.q; } // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── // Rys root computation // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── /// Compute Rys quadrature roots and weights for the given T value. /// /// This is a convenience wrapper around [rys_roots_weights] from the /// eri_rys module. The Rys parameter is T = rho * |P - Q|², where /// rho = p*q/(p+q) is the reduced exponent and |P - Q|² is the /// squared distance between the bra and ket product centers. /// /// # Arguments /// /// * t — The Rys parameter T = rho * R_PQ², must be non-negative. /// * nroots — Number of quadrature points (= Rys order). /// /// # Returns /// /// A tuple (roots, weights) of length nroots each. /// /// # Examples /// /// /// use poler_eri::shell_driver::compute_rys_roots; /// /// let (roots, weights) = compute_rys_roots(1.0, 1); /// assert_eq!(roots.len(), 1); /// assert!(roots[0] >= 0.0 && roots[0] <= 1.0); /// assert!(weights[0] > 0.0); /// pub fn compute_rys_roots(t: f64, nroots: usize) -> (Vec<f64>, Vec<f64>) { rys_roots_weights(t, nroots) } // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── // Main entry point // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── /// Compute ALL Cartesian component ERIs for a shell quartet (single primitive). /// /// This is the main entry point for the shell driver. It computes all /// ncart(la) * ncart(lb) * ncart(lc) * ncart(ld) ERI values for the /// specified primitive quartet. /// /// # Algorithm /// /// 1. Build the ShellQuartetDriver for the given angular momenta. /// 2. Compute Rys roots and weights for T = rho * |P - Q|². /// 3. For each Rys root, evaluate the circuit for directions x, y, z. /// 4. Extract I(na, nb | nc, nd) for each Cartesian component and accumulate ///    w_k * I_x * I_y * I_z. /// 5. Multiply by prefactor * K_ab * K_cd. /// /// # Ordering /// /// The result array uses row-major ordering with bra indices varying slowest: /// /// text /// result[ia * stride_a + ib * stride_b + ic * stride_c + id] ///  /// /// where: /// - stride_a = ncart(lb) * ncart(lc) * ncart(ld) /// - stride_b = ncart(lc) * ncart(ld) /// - stride_c = ncart(ld) /// - stride_d = 1 /// /// # Arguments /// /// * qd — Precomputed geometric data for the primitive quartet. /// * la — Angular momentum on center A (0=s, 1=p, 2=d, ...). /// * lb — Angular momentum on center B. /// * lc — Angular momentum on center C. /// * ld — Angular momentum on center D. /// /// # Returns /// /// A flat array of ERI values in row-major order. /// /// # Examples /// /// /// use poler_eri::{QuartetData, Point}; /// use poler_eri::shell_driver::eri_shell_full; /// /// // (ss|ss) quartet: single integral /// let qd = QuartetData::new( ///     Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), ///     Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), Point([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), ///     1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, /// ); /// let eris = eri_shell_full(&qd, 0, 0, 0, 0); /// assert_eq!(eris.len(), 1); /// assert!(eris[0] > 0.0); /// pub fn eri_shell_full(qd: &QuartetData, la: usize, lb: usize, lc: usize, ld: usize) -> Vec<f64> { let driver = ShellQuartetDriver::new(la, lb, lc, ld); driver.compute(qd) } // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── // Tests // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; } \n---\n\n### poler-eri/src/eri_rys.rs ⚠️ Этот файл очень большой (>1000 строк) — содержит прямую порту rys_root1/2/3/4 из libcint. Исходный код: poler-dynamis\n\n### poler-dynamis/src/gto_utils.rs\n\n`rust // FILE: /home/z/my-project/poler-unified/poler-dynamis/src/gto_utils.rs //! gto_utils.rs — Модуль нормализации Гауссовых примитивов //! //! Устраняет дублирование между cint_gto_norm() и gto_normalization() //! в basis_parser.rs. //! //! # Математическая основа //! //! Нормализационный коэффициент для радиальной части GTO g = r^l * exp(-alpha * r^2): //! //! text //! N_l(alpha) = 1 / sqrt( integral_0^inf [r^(2l) * exp(-2*alpha*r^2)]^2 * r^2 dr ) //! = 1 / sqrt( gaussian_int(2l+2, 2*alpha) ) //! //! //! где gaussian_int — гауссов интеграл: //! //! text //! integral_0^inf r^n * exp(-a*r^2) dr = Gamma((n+1)/2) / (2 * a^((n+1)/2)) //! //! //! Использование libm::lgamma (логарифма гамма-функции) обеспечивает: //! - Численную стабильность при высоких l (l >= 6, i/k-орбитали) //! - Отсутствие переполнения integer (в отличие от double_factorial) //! - Кросс-платформенную совместимость без extern “C” FFI /// Безопасная обёртка над lgamma через libm. /// /// libm::lgamma(x) возвращает log(|Gamma(x)|), что обеспечивает /// численную стабильность при высоких угловых моментах. #[inline] fn lgamma_rs(x: f64) -> f64 { libm::lgamma(x) } /// Вычисление гауссова интеграла: /// /// text /// integral_0^inf r^n * exp(-a * r^2) dr = Gamma((n+1)/2) / (2 * a^((n+1)/2)) /// /// /// Использует lgamma для высокой численной стабильности. #[inline] fn gaussian_int(n: i64, alpha: f64) -> f64 { let n1 = (n as f64 + 1.0) * 0.5; lgamma_rs(n1).exp() / (2.0 * alpha.powf(n1)) } /// Нормализация GTO радиальной части. /// /// text /// N_l(alpha) = 1 / sqrt( gaussian_int(2l+2, 2*alpha) ) /// /// /// # Arguments /// /// * l — Угловой момент (0=s, 1=p, 2=d, 3=f, …) /// * alpha — Экспонента Гауссова примитива /// /// # Returns /// /// Нормализационный коэффициент N_l(alpha) pub fn gto_normalization(l: u8, alpha: f64) -> f64 { if alpha <= 0.0 { return 0.0; } 1.0 / gaussian_int(2 * l as i64 + 2, 2.0 * alpha).sqrt() } /// Псевдоним для совместимости. /// /// Идемпотентен: cint_gto_norm(l, alpha) == gto_normalization(l, alpha). pub fn cint_gto_norm(l: u8, alpha: f64) -> f64 { gto_normalization(l, alpha) } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; } —### poler-dynamis/src/energy_engine.rs// FILE: /home/z/my-project/poler-unified/poler-dynamis/src/energy_engine.rs //! energy_engine.rs — The HEART of the POLER quantum chemistry engine //! //! Implements the canonical equation of motion: //! //! text //! DM_{t+1} = Π_Λ( DM_t − η(t) · [Δ_idem + γ(t)·J·DM + K] ) //! ``` //! //! where: //! - η(t) = η₀·exp(−β·Σ_true) is the adaptive learning rate (thermostat) //! - Π_Λ = McWeeny retraction (3DM² − 2DM³)/occ_max applied AFTER Euler step //! - Δ_idem = d·(DM² − occ_max·DM) is the idempotency dissipator //! - J = j·(A − A^T) where A = Σ_k P_k · ΔP_k^T (temporal echo R[n]) //! - γ(t) = γ₀·exp(−α_σ·Σ)·(1 − t/T_max)² (Feynman annealing) //! - K = F·DM·S − S·DM·F is the orbital gradient //! - Σ_true = ||ΔK||_F / ||ΔDM||_F (secant Hessian approximation) //! //! Uses faer::Mat exclusively. Eigendecomposition via faer’s hermitian EVD //! (fast O(n²·log n) tridiagonal QR, replacing the slow O(n³) cyclic Jacobi). use faer::{scale, Col, Mat, Parallelism}; use faer::linalg::evd::{compute_hermitian_evd, compute_hermitian_evd_req, ComputeVectors, HermitianEvdParams}; use faer::dyn_stack::PodStack; // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Evolution State — Ring Buffer for Temporal Echo R[n] // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// Evolution state tracking DM and K history for resonance computation. /// /// Stores a ring buffer of recent density matrices and orbital gradient matrices, /// enabling the temporal echo operator R[n] (resonance J) to compute the /// cross-correlation integral A = Σ P_t · ΔP_t^T. pub struct EvolutionState { /// Ring buffer of recent DM matrices (most recent last). dm_history: Vec<Mat>, /// Ring buffer of recent K (orbital gradient) matrices. k_history: Vec<Mat>, /// Maximum depth of history to retain. max_depth: usize, } impl EvolutionState { /// Create a new evolution state with the given maximum history depth. pub fn new(max_depth: usize) -> Self { Self { dm_history: Vec::with_capacity(max_depth + 1), k_history: Vec::with_capacity(max_depth + 1), max_depth, } } } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // DIIS (Direct Inversion in Iterative Subspace) — kept for bootstrap only // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// DIIS state for SCF bootstrap acceleration (Phase 1 only). /// /// DIIS is used ONLY during the initial bootstrap phase to rapidly bring /// the DM into the correct orbital subspace. Once the POLER-flow takes over /// (Phase 2), the temporal echo operator J replaces DIIS entirely. pub struct DiisState { fock_history: Vec<Mat>, error_history: Vec<Mat>, max_size: usize, min_overlap: f64, } impl DiisState { pub fn new(max_size: usize) -> Self { Self { fock_history: Vec::with_capacity(max_size + 1), error_history: Vec::with_capacity(max_size + 1), max_size, min_overlap: 1e-12, } } } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Configuration & Result Structures // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// POLER engine configuration parameters. #[derive(Debug, Clone)] pub struct PolerConfig { // ── Adaptive step η(t) = η₀ · exp(−β_σ · Σ_true) ── /// Initial learning rate. pub eta0: f64, /// Damping factor β_σ for adaptive η: controls how strongly /// topological curvature slows the system. pub beta_sigma: f64, } impl Default for PolerConfig { fn default() -> Self { Self { eta0: 0.3, beta_sigma: 3.0, // Curvature damping for η idem_strength: 0.2, // Dissipator strength resonance_gamma0: 0.05, // Initial resonance coupling resonance_j: 0.01, // Resonance matrix scale alpha_sigma: 2.0, // Curvature damping for γ resonance_depth: 8, // History depth for temporal echo mcweeny_order: 1, // Mild retraction per step occ_max: 2.0, nelec: 2.0, max_iter: 500, conv_tol: 1e-8, phase1_steps: 30, // DIIS bootstrap only diis_max_vectors: 6, level_shift: 0.0, // No shift by default; use 0.3 for Li chains } } } /// POLER convergence result. #[derive(Debug, Clone)] pub struct PolerResult { /// Final density matrix. pub dm: Mat, /// Final Fock matrix. pub fock: Mat, /// Electronic energy E = 0.5·(Tr[H·DM] + Tr[F·DM]). pub energy: f64, /// Total iterations performed. pub iterations: usize, /// Whether the engine converged within conv_tol. pub converged: bool, /// Frobenius norm of the final orbital gradient K. pub gradient_norm: f64, /// History of orbital gradient norms ||K||_F per iteration. pub gradient_history: Vec, /// History of learning rate η per iteration. pub eta_history: Vec, /// History of topological curvature Σ per iteration. pub curvature_history: Vec, /// History of resonance coupling γ per iteration. pub gamma_history: Vec, /// History of electronic energy per iteration. pub energy_history: Vec, /// Phase label per iteration: “P1” = DIIS, “P2” = POLER-flow. pub phase_history: Vec, } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Utility Functions // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// Compute the Frobenius norm of a matrix: ||M||_F = sqrt(Σ_ij M_ij²). pub fn frobenius_norm(m: &Mat) -> f64 { let mut sum = 0.0f64; for i in 0..m.nrows() { for j in 0..m.ncols() { let v = m[(i, j)]; sum += v * v; } } sum.sqrt() } /// Compute the trace of the matrix product A·B: Tr[A·B] = Σ_i (AB)_ii. pub fn trace_product(a: &Mat, b: &Mat) -> f64 { let n = a.nrows(); let mut tr = 0.0f64; for i in 0..n { for k in 0..n { tr += a[(i, k)] * b[(k, i)]; } } tr } /// Symmetrize a matrix: M_sym = 0.5·(M + M^T). pub fn symmetrize(dm: &Mat) -> Mat { let n = dm.nrows(); let mut result = Mat::zeros(n, n); for i in 0..n { for j in 0..n { result[(i, j)] = 0.5 * (dm[(i, j)] + dm[(j, i)]); } } result } /// Matrix subtraction: A − B. fn mat_sub(a: &Mat, b: &Mat) -> Mat { let (r, c) = (a.nrows(), a.ncols()); let mut result = Mat::zeros(r, c); for i in 0..r { for j in 0..c { result[(i, j)] = a[(i, j)] - b[(i, j)]; } } result } /// Matrix transpose. fn transpose(m: &Mat) -> Mat { let (r, c) = (m.nrows(), m.ncols()); let mut t = Mat::zeros(c, r); for i in 0..r { for j in 0..c { t[(j, i)] = m[(i, j)]; } } t } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Jacobi Eigendecomposition for Symmetric Matrices // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// Cyclic Jacobi eigendecomposition for a real symmetric matrix. /// /// Returns (eigenvalues, eigenvectors) where eigenvectors are stored as /// columns of the output matrix. Eigenvalues are sorted in ascending order. /// /// DEPRECATED: Kept as a fallback reference. Use sym_eigen instead for /// ~10-100× speedup on large matrices via faer’s tridiagonal QR algorithm. #[allow(dead_code)] fn jacobi_eigen(mat: &Mat, max_sweeps: usize, tol: f64) -> (Vec, Mat) { let n = mat.nrows(); assert_eq!(n, mat.ncols(), “jacobi_eigen requires a square matrix”); } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Fast Symmetric Eigendecomposition via faer’s Hermitian EVD // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// Fast symmetric eigendecomposition using faer’s hermitian EVD. /// /// Uses the tridiagonal reduction + QR algorithm pathway, which is O(n²·log n) /// compared to the O(n³) cyclic Jacobi. Returns (eigenvalues_sorted_ascending, /// eigenvectors_as_columns). /// /// Note: faer’s hermitian EVD accesses only the LOWER triangular part of the /// input matrix. For numerical robustness, we symmetrize the input before /// decomposition to avoid issues with asymmetric floating-point residuals. /// /// This replaces jacobi_eigen for all production use. The Jacobi method is /// retained as #[allow(dead_code)] for reference/testing only. pub fn sym_eigen(mat: &Mat) -> (Vec, Mat) { let n = mat.nrows(); assert_eq!(n, mat.ncols(), “sym_eigen requires a square matrix”); } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Core Quantum Chemistry Functions // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// McWeeny purification: DM_pure = (3/occ_max)·DM² − (2/occ_max²)·DM³ /// /// This is the retraction operator Π_Λ that enforces idempotency DM² = occ_max·DM. /// Applied order times for stronger purification. pub fn mcweeny_purify(dm: &Mat, occ_max: f64, order: usize) -> Mat { let c1 = 3.0 / occ_max; let c2 = 2.0 / (occ_max * occ_max); } /// Compute the idempotency dissipator Δ_idem = d·(DM² − occ_max·DM). /// /// This term drives the density matrix toward idempotency through a /// dissipative force. It annihilates (becomes zero) when DM is exactly idempotent. pub fn compute_idem_dissipator(dm: &Mat, d: f64, occ_max: f64) -> Mat { let dm_sq = dm * dm; let mut result = Mat::zeros(dm.nrows(), dm.ncols()); for i in 0..dm.nrows() { for j in 0..dm.ncols() { result[(i, j)] = d * (dm_sq[(i, j)] - occ_max * dm[(i, j)]); } } result } /// Compute the orbital gradient K = F·DM·S − S·DM·F. /// /// This is the generalized commutator that vanishes at convergence: /// K = 0 ⟺ [F, DM]*S = 0 ⟺ DM is stationary. pub fn compute_orbital_gradient(fock: &Mat, dm: &Mat, s: &Mat) -> Mat { let fds = fock * dm * s; let sdf = s * dm * fock; &fds - &sdf } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Equation 5: Resonance Operator J — Temporal Echo R[n] // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// Compute the resonance matrix J = j·(A − A^T) from DM history. /// /// The matrix A is the cross-correlation integral of past states and their /// velocity (change) vectors: /// /// A = (1/N) Σ_k P_k · ΔP_k^T /// /// where ΔP_k = P*{k+1} − P_k is the velocity (analog of momentum in /// classical mechanics). The skew-symmetric part J = j·(A − A^T) generates /// phase angular momentum on the Grassmann manifold, enabling the system /// to tunnel through local minima via temporal interference of past states. /// /// For RHF with symmetric DM, the old implementation A = DM·DM^T gave /// A − A^T ≡ 0. This corrected version uses the velocity history instead. pub fn compute_resonance( dm_history: &[Mat], j_strength: f64, depth: usize, ) -> Mat { if dm_history.len() < 2 || j_strength.abs() < 1e-15 { let n = if dm_history.is_empty() { 1 } else { dm_history[0].nrows() }; return Mat::zeros(n, n); } } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Equation 6: True Topological Curvature Σ (Secant Hessian) // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// Compute the true topological curvature Σ = ||ΔK||_F / ||ΔDM||_F. /// /// This is a secant approximation to the orbital Hessian ∂²E/∂DM². /// Unlike the old “surprise” (||[F,DM]||*F, which is a gradient not a curvature), /// this quantity correctly measures the dynamic resistance of the energy landscape: /// /// - When the HOMO-LUMO gap is near zero (metallic systems like Li₅₀), /// even tiny DM changes cause huge gradient swings → Σ → ∞ → η → 0 /// (system automatically slows down in degenerate zones) /// - When the system is in a smooth basin, Σ is modest → η stays large /// /// Returns 0.0 if ΔDM is negligibly small (absolute rest). pub fn compute_topological_curvature( k_current: &Mat, k_prev: &Mat, dm_current: &Mat, dm_prev: &Mat, ) -> f64 { let delta_k = mat_sub(k_current, k_prev); let delta_dm = mat_sub(dm_current, dm_prev); } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Equation 6: Adaptive Resonance γ(t) — Feynman Annealing // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// Compute the adaptive resonance coupling γ(t). /// /// Two mechanisms combined: /// 1. Thermodynamic damping: γ_thermo = γ₀ · exp(−α_σ · Σ) /// When curvature is high (frustration), the resonance is damped /// to prevent the system from being ejected from narrow attractor throats. /// /// 2. Feynman annealing: γ_anneal = (1 − t/T_max)² /// Quadratic schedule that gradually freezes oscillations, /// allowing final crystallization (phase Ψ, H_Ψ = 0). /// /// Combined: γ(t) = γ₀ · exp(−α_σ · Σ) · (1 − t/T_max)² pub fn compute_gamma_t( gamma0: f64, alpha_sigma: f64, sigma_true: f64, current_step: usize, max_steps: usize, ) -> f64 { // 1. Thermodynamic damping through curvature let gamma_thermo = gamma0 * (-alpha_sigma * sigma_true).exp(); } /// Adaptive learning rate: η(t) = η₀ · exp(−β · Σ_true). /// /// Returns the new η, clamped to [1e-6, 2.0] for numerical safety. pub fn adaptive_eta(sigma_true: f64, eta0: f64, beta: f64) -> f64 { (eta0 * (-beta * sigma_true).exp()).clamp(1e-6, 2.0) } /// Compute the POLER free energy: E = 0.5·(Tr[H_core·DM] + Tr[F·DM]). pub fn compute_free_energy(h_core: &Mat, fock: &Mat, dm: &Mat) -> f64 { 0.5 * (trace_product(h_core, dm) + trace_product(fock, dm)) } /// Ensure the density matrix has the correct electron count. /// /// Scales DM so that Tr[DM·S] = nelec. pub fn ensure_electron_count(dm: &Mat, s: &Mat, nelec: f64) -> Mat { let ds = dm * s; let mut current_nelec = 0.0f64; for i in 0..ds.nrows() { current_nelec += ds[(i, i)]; } if current_nelec.abs() < 1e-14 { return dm.clone(); } let scale_factor = nelec / current_nelec; let mut result = dm.clone(); for i in 0..result.nrows() { for j in 0..result.ncols() { result[(i, j)] *= scale_factor; } } result } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Overlap Inverse Square Root & DM Construction // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// Compute S^{-1/2} = U · diag(s^{-1/2}) · U^T from the overlap matrix S. fn compute_sinv_half(s: &Mat) -> Mat { let n = s.nrows(); let (s_evals, s_evecs) = sym_eigen(s); } /// Build the density matrix from a Fock matrix via Roothaan-Hall diagonalization. /// /// If level_shift > 0, adds a shift to virtual orbital eigenvalues before /// building the DM. This creates an artificial gap that stabilizes metallic /// systems (e.g., Li chains) by preventing orbital scrambling between nearly /// degenerate occupied and virtual states. /// /// The level shift is equivalent to adding shift * (I - P_occ) to the Fock /// matrix in the orthogonal basis, where P_occ is the occupied subspace projector. /// This stabilizes WHICH orbitals are occupied without changing the final energy. fn build_dm_from_fock( fock: &Mat, sinv_half: &Mat, nelec: f64, occ_max: f64, level_shift: f64, ) -> Mat { let n = fock.nrows(); let nocc = (nelec / occ_max) as usize; } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // POLER Engine // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ /// The main POLER quantum chemistry engine. /// /// Implements the canonical equation of motion: /// /// text /// DM*{t+1} = Π_Λ( DM_t − η(t) · [Δ_idem + γ(t)·J·DM + K] ) /// /// /// Phase 1 (bootstrap): DIIS-accelerated SCF to rapidly bring DM /// into the correct orbital subspace. /// /// Phase 2 (POLER-flow): The full canonical equation with: /// - Adaptive step η(t) = η₀·exp(−β·Σ_true) /// - True topological curvature Σ = ||ΔK||/||ΔDM|| /// - Temporal echo J from DM history ring buffer /// - Feynman-annealed resonance γ(t) = γ₀·exp(−α·Σ)·(1−t/T)² /// - McWeeny retraction Π_Λ after each Euler step pub struct PolerEngine { pub config: PolerConfig, } impl PolerEngine { pub fn new(config: PolerConfig) -> Self { Self { config } } } // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ // Tests // ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use
